name: Rethymno Old Town
seoTitle: Rethymno Old Town: What to See, the Fortezza and Venetian Harbour
seoDescription: Rethymno Old Town is the best-preserved Venetian and Ottoman quarter in Crete: the Fortezza, the Rimondi Fountain of 1626, Porta Guora and the Venetian harbour.
summary: Rethymno Old Town is the best-preserved Renaissance quarter in Crete, a compact grid of Venetian and Ottoman streets on the north coast between the Fortezza fortress and a small Venetian harbour with a lighthouse. Nothing in it needs a ticket: the landmarks are the Rimondi Fountain, built in 1626, Porta Guora, the last surviving gate of the city walls, the Neratze Mosque with its minaret, and the harbour itself, all within a ten-minute walk of each other. Venetian doorways, wooden Ottoman balconies and minarets sit above ordinary shops and cafes, and the quarter is still lived in rather than preserved for visitors.
body:
## The layout

The old town occupies a headland. The Fortezza, the Venetian fortress begun in 1573, closes the northern end; the Venetian harbour with its lighthouse sits on the east side; Porta Guora marks the southern edge where the walls once ran. Everything in between is walkable in twenty minutes if you do not stop, which nobody does.

## What to look for

**The Rimondi Fountain**, 1626, built by the Venetian rector Alvise Rimondi: three lion heads pouring water between Corinthian columns, in a small square that is still the meeting point of the quarter.

**Porta Guora**, the only piece of the city wall left standing, an arched gate that separates the old town from the modern one.

**The Neratze Mosque**, a Venetian church converted after the Ottoman conquest of 1646 and given the tallest minaret in Crete. It now serves as the city's music school and concert hall.

**The Fortezza**, one of the largest Venetian castles built, with a ticketed circuit of walls, the domed Sultan Ibrahim Mosque inside, and views over the sea and the town.

**The Venetian harbour**, small, curved and lined with tavernas, with the Egyptian-built lighthouse of the 1830s at its mouth.

## Eating

Rethymno is the strongest food town in the region and much of it is in the old quarter: bakeries selling kalitsounia and lichnarakia, the Chatziparaschos family workshop where filo and kataifi have been made by hand for more than sixty years, and tavernas in the back streets that are not on the harbour front and cost half as much.

## Practicalities

The old town is pedestrianised in large part and free to walk. The Fortezza charges admission. Cars are best left in the car parks on the edge; the streets inside are narrow, one-way and awkward. Early morning is the time to photograph it without people in the frame.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Rethymno Old Town?
faqs.a: The Fortezza fortress, the Rimondi Fountain of 1626, Porta Guora, the Neratze Mosque and its minaret, and the Venetian harbour with its lighthouse. All of them are within a ten-minute walk of each other and only the Fortezza charges admission.

faqs.q: Is Rethymno Old Town free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. The streets, the fountain, the gate and the harbour are all free. The Fortezza has its own entrance fee.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Rethymno Old Town?
faqs.a: Half a day covers the landmarks at a walking pace with a coffee stop. A guided food walk through it typically runs four hours, ending with lunch.

faqs.q: Why does it look Venetian and Ottoman at the same time?
faqs.a: Because it is both. Venice held Rethymno from 1204 until the Ottoman siege of 1646, and the Ottomans then ruled until 1898. Rather than rebuild, they converted: churches became mosques, minarets went up beside Venetian facades, and wooden balconies were added to existing houses.

faqs.q: Can you drive into the old town?
faqs.a: Barely, and it is not worth trying. Much of it is pedestrianised and the rest is narrow and one-way. Use one of the car parks on the edge of the quarter and walk in.
